newsitem.title: HAITI: Hundreds in Haiti homeless from fires tied to dumping.
newsitem.headline: Hundreds in Haiti homeless from fires tied to dumping.

text.p: Wilson Pierre was sleeping in his tiny tin house in the giant seaside slum Cite Soleil this week when he heard someone screaming "Fire!"
Before dawn Thursday, he awoke to find his house and others along a wide, stinking canal going up in flames, with no way to put them out.
"We tried to throw water on it, but the canal is filled with oil, so it only got worse," he said.
The fire was the fifth of its kind in about two weeks in Cite Soleil, a slum that is home to more than 200,000 of the very poorest people in the hemisphere's poorest nation.

The conditions in Cite Soleil, made worse by the raging fires, exemplify the huge tasks faced by Haiti's government and the international community since an international force sent 20,000 troops to the Caribbean nation two years ago to restore its freely elected government.

With an unemployment rate above 65 percent and an annual per capita income of only about $270, Haiti offers what Americans would consider a reasonable standard of living to very few of its more than 7 million people, although it lies only about 625 miles (1,000 km) from Miami, closer to the Florida city than New York.

In the giant slums of the nation's capital, unemployment and illiteracy are virtually universal, and services like telephones and electricity are non-existent. Slum dwellers' homes are shacks crowded around the fetid canals that carry Port-au-Prince's sewage to the sea.
And on top of this misery come fires that this month have left hundreds of families without even those shacks.
Residents blame raw oil residues in the canals and say it comes from Electricite d'Haiti, the national elctric company located just up the hill from Cite Soleil.

Officials with the state-owned electric company -- which provides power to only 6 percent of Haitians and is slated to be privatised under a massive government reorganization advocated by President Rene Preval -- Saturday said there was no proof the fires were caused by the oil.
But Wilson Pierre said one look at the black ooze in the canal next to the burned remains of his home is proof enough of a problem.

"We have asked them to stop dumping the oil," he said to enthusiastic nods from his neighbours. "We have children here and not only is it a fire hazard, but it is bad for everyone's health -- including the rich people who may not live here but eat fish from the sea."
Power plant manager Jean Marie Joseph Lefranc broke from the official line and said oil residue -- a mix of gas, oil, grease and water -- does flow from the plant into the slum.
"We are waiting for another piece to fix the treatment reservoir, and we have a pump that doesn't work," he said.
U.N. officials said they might intervene with the peacekeeping troops posted in Haiti for two years.

"Either we need to go in there and pressure the company to stop dumping, or assist them with the technology if they are not capable," said one high level U.N. official, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Joseph Lefranc said the company would solve the problem, but Cite Soleil residents demanded immediate action.
"Maybe we need to go to the plant with some matches and show them what it is like to have everything you own burned down," said one angry victim of a fire this week.
Victims of a previous fire nearly did just that last week, burning tires in front of the plant to draw attention after the government did not respond to their complaints.

Prime Minister Rosny Smarth visited the scene of the first fire in late November after about 300 homes were destroyed. But he won few friends as he stepped from his air conditioned vehicle in a crisp suit and held his nose as he walked past the burned homes along the sewer canal.
"He was holding his nose!" exclaimed one woman, remembering the visit. "How does he think it is for us? We live here and don't even notice the smell and we breath the unhealthy air."
